title: Cold & Flu Relief

drivers.name: Price increase (6.2%)
drivers.evidence: Price rose from $11.33 to $12.03. Past promotions (discounts) had x1.4 noise-adjusted lift; price hikes likely have inverse effect. No direct evidence, but 12% downward effect is plausible given elasticity.

drivers.name: Heatwave (38°C)
drivers.evidence: No historical data on heatwave-weeks, but product sales spiked during back-to-school and holidays. Heat may drive preventative purchase. Evidence is weak (one event, no prior data), so effect shrunk to 15%.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 19.0. A 6.2% price increase to $12.03 is a known demand-lowering driver. Past promotions (avg. 30% off) lifted sales by x1.4 (noise-adjusted), but this is a price hike, not a discount. The week after a promotion typically sees x0.76 sales (noise-adjusted x1.0), but no promotion preceded this week. The heatwave (38°C) may boost cold/flu product demand as a preventative measure. No historical heatwave-week data exists, but the product has seasonal spikes (e.g., back-to-school, Labor Day). The baseline trend is down (-11.8% over 13 weeks), but the heatwave may override this. The classical model suggests no uplift, but judgment favors a modest increase. Evidence is thin, so shrink toward 1.0.

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 19.0 | 5%-95%: 7.2 - 34.4 | 10%-90%: 10.3 - 30.9

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-46% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
